summary: Pupils aged 12-14 learn that when a transversal crosses a pair of parallel lines it produces a structured set of equal and supplementary angles: corresponding angles are equal, alternate (interior) angles are equal, and co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary (sum to 180°). The aim is to REASON with these relationships to find unknown angles and to justify WHY they hold — grounding equality in the translation of one crossing's four-angle cluster along the transversal onto the other, rather than in a memorised 'F' or 'Z' shape. Teaching must separate the equal family (corresponding, alternate) from the supplementary family (co-interior), insist on precise language and full reasons, and use off-set and rotated diagrams so pupils still perceive genuinely parallel lines as parallel and apply the rules.
misconceptions: Over-generalising 'angles on parallel lines are equal', so treating co-interior (supplementary) angles as equal
Confusing alternate and corresponding angles, and failing to identify them in non-standard diagrams
Relying on 'F'/'Z' mnemonics that give the answer without supporting reasoning
Not perceiving off-set lines (little overlap) as parallel, so not applying the angle rules
Applying parallel-line angle rules to lines that are not actually parallel

activities.title: Translate the angle cluster along the transversal
steps: Draw (or use a prepared diagram of) two parallel lines crossed by a transversal, marking the parallels with matching arrows.
Trace the four-angle cluster at the upper crossing onto tracing paper, then slide the tracing straight down along the transversal until it lands on the lower crossing.

Observe that every angle in the slid copy lands on the matching angle at the lower crossing (as closely as tracing allows; in the ideal diagram the fit is exact). State which pairs this shows are equal: corresponding angles directly, and alternate angles by combining this with vertically opposite angles at the same crossing.
Now draw a second diagram where one line is deliberately NOT parallel to the other; trace and slide again, and record where the copy fails to fit and how the readings differ.
Write a one-sentence conclusion: equality of these angle pairs depends on the lines being parallel.
activities.insight: Corresponding angles are equal because one crossing's angle cluster can be translated along the transversal onto the other, which is a transformation, not a shape to recognise. Alternate angles are then equal because each one is vertically opposite a corresponding partner. These equalities break when the lines are not parallel.

activities.title: Sort angle pairs into equal and supplementary families
steps: In a given parallel-lines-and-transversal diagram, point to one marked angle (e.g. 70°) and name its corresponding, alternate, and co-interior partners.
Colour the equal family (corresponding and alternate) in one hue and the supplementary family (co-interior) in another.
For a 70° starting angle, label each partner with its value: the equal partners read 70°, and the co-interior partner reads 110° because co-interior angles sum to 180° (180 − 70 = 110).
Explain in words why the co-interior angle is 110° and not 70°, referring to the straight line or to the equal angle that sits on a straight line with it.
activities.insight: Not all angles made with parallel lines are equal: corresponding and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles are supplementary, so a 70° angle produces both 70° partners and a 110° partner.

activities.title: Identify pairs in off-set and rotated diagrams
steps: Work with diagrams where the parallel lines overlap only a little, are off-set, or are rotated away from the usual horizontal layout, with the parallels marked by arrows.
Before applying any rule, check the arrow marks to confirm the lines really are parallel.
Pick out and name each requested angle pair (corresponding, alternate, co-interior) despite the unusual orientation.
Also examine a diagram whose lines are NOT marked parallel and explain why the equal/supplementary rules may not apply there.
activities.insight: Parallelism is judged by the marking arrows and definition, not by how similar the lines look; the angle relationships hold in rotated and off-set diagrams whenever the lines are genuinely parallel, and must not be assumed when they are not.

activities.title: Multi-step angle chase with a stated reason at each step
steps: Given a diagram combining parallel lines, a transversal, and other lines, find an unknown angle that requires two or more steps.
At each step, write the angle fact used as a full reason, e.g. 'x = 45° because alternate angles are equal' or 'y = 180 − 45 = 135° because angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Use secure basic facts where needed: angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal, and angles at a point sum to 360°.
Check the final answer by an independent route (e.g. a different pair of angles) where possible.
activities.insight: Unknown angles are found by chaining relationships, each justified by a stated reason, building on secure basic angle facts rather than by pattern-matching a letter shape.

activities.title: Predict, reason, then check (diagnostic)
steps: Look at two parallel lines cut by a transversal with one angle marked 70°; the teacher points to its co-interior (same-side interior) angle.
PREDICT whether that angle is equal, bigger, or smaller than 70°, and state WHY before checking.
Check by sliding a tracing-paper copy of the 70° angle (or an equal partner) along the transversal and reasoning via the straight line: the co-interior angle is 180 − 70 = 110°.
Answer the follow-up: would the answer still hold if the lines were not quite parallel, and why does parallelism matter?
activities.insight: Co-interior angles between parallel lines are supplementary (110° here), distinct from the equal alternate/corresponding pairs; a correct justification distinguishes the two families and depends on the lines being parallel.

checkQuestion: In this diagram two parallel lines are crossed by a transversal. One angle is marked 70°. The angle I point to is its co-interior (same-side interior) angle. What is that angle, and explain how you know.
checkAnswer: 110°. Co-interior (same-side interior) angles between parallel lines are supplementary — they add to 180° — so 180 − 70 = 110°. (Equivalently, the 70° angle is equal to the alternate/corresponding angle that sits on a straight line with the co-interior angle, and angles on a straight line sum to 180°.) The reasoning must distinguish co-interior/supplementary from the equal alternate/corresponding pairs.
